/work/kunsthal-nord.title: Kunsthal Nord, Yassin Farag
/work/kunsthal-nord.description: Wayfinding for a concrete art hall where every floor looks the same and visitors kept ending up in the car park.
p: Wayfinding for a concrete art hall where every floor looks the same and visitors kept ending up in the car park.
Kunsthal Nord is four floors of identical board-marked concrete. Visitors couldn’t tell one level from another, and the lifts opened onto blank walls.
The hall wanted signs that respected the building instead of covering it.

Every level got one oversized marker painted straight onto the concrete, and every direction got one thin arrow. Nothing is lit and nothing is coloured, so the art stays the loudest thing in the room.
Help-desk questions about directions dropped by half in the first three months after opening.

/work/osk-audio.title: Osk Audio, Yassin Farag
/work/osk-audio.description: Brand identity and launch site for a small speaker company that wanted to sound expensive without looking loud.
p: Brand identity and launch site for a small speaker company that wanted to sound expensive without looking loud.
Osk had one product, a machined aluminium speaker, and a launch date eleven weeks away.

The identity takes its cues from the grille: a tight perforated pattern, a graphite palette, and one orange pull tab that became the brand’s only accent. The launch site is a single page that moves at the pace of the product photography.
The copy stays short and specific: what it is, how it sounds, what it costs.
The first production run sold out within a week of launch.

/work/mork-roasters.title: Mørk Roasters, Yassin Farag
/work/mork-roasters.description: A quiet identity for a small-batch roaster that wanted its bags to look as dark as the coffee inside them.
p: A quiet identity for a small-batch roaster that wanted its bags to look as dark as the coffee inside them.
Mørk roasts in small batches and sells mostly to cafés. Their old bags were kraft paper with a sticker, and every café already had three of those on the shelf.
They wanted packaging a barista would reach for without reading it.
We went black on black. The bag is matte, the mark is a single gloss stroke, and the roast date is printed large in the only white on the pack, because that is the one thing customers actually check.
Mørk now ships to forty cafés across Norway, and the black bag has become the thing people photograph first.

/work/lumen-line.title: Lumen Line, Yassin Farag
/work/lumen-line.description: A wayfinding system for a new light rail line, built around one rule: you should be able to read it while walking.
p: A wayfinding system for a new light rail line, built around one rule: you should be able to read it while walking.
A new line of eleven stops, platforms that are partly underground, and riders who have never used it before.
Every sign answers one question. Direction comes first, as a single large arrow. The line colour, a signal orange, runs as a light strip so a platform can be found from the street at night.
Full-size prototypes were tested on site with riders before anything was fabricated.
The system is now the operator’s standard for its next two lines.

/work/nordvik-ceramics.title: Nordvik Ceramics, Yassin Farag
/work/nordvik-ceramics.description: Identity and online store for a two-person stoneware studio, with photography that lets the glazes do the talking.
p: Identity and online store for a two-person stoneware studio, with photography that lets the glazes do the talking.
Nordvik’s pots sold out at markets but barely moved online. Product photos were taken on a kitchen table and the store ran on a default theme.

A small kit: one dark plinth, one light, one lens. Every piece is shot the same way, so the glaze is the only variable. The store follows the same restraint, with one column and nothing competing with the work.
Packaging is kraft paper, black tissue and a blank seal. Cheap to produce, easy to pack by hand.
Online sales now carry the studio through its quiet months, and the shooting kit lets them photograph a new batch in an afternoon.

/work/parallel-archive.title: Parallel Archive, Yassin Farag
/work/parallel-archive.description: A website for a private archive of post-war architecture, designed to feel like turning pages instead of scrolling a feed.
p: A website for a private archive of post-war architecture, designed to feel like turning pages instead of scrolling a feed.
Parallel holds tens of thousands of photographs and drawings of post-war buildings, most of them never published. Their old site was a search box and a wall of thumbnails.
Each collection is treated as a printed book: a strict grid, generous margins and one image at a time. Search still exists, but the default way in is a curated sequence.
The plaster models in the archive’s studio became the photographic language, lit from one side to match the archive’s own photographs.
Visitors now stay with one collection instead of bouncing between thumbnails, and the archive uses the same grid for its printed catalogues.

/work/halden-acoustics.title: Halden Acoustics, Yassin Farag
/work/halden-acoustics.description: Identity and packaging for an Oslo maker of wool acoustic panels, built from the grooves in their own product.
p: Identity and packaging for an Oslo maker of wool acoustic panels, built from the grooves in their own product.
Halden makes acoustic panels from recycled wool felt. Architects liked the product but couldn’t find it: the company looked like every other building supplier, with a stock logo and grey PDFs.
They needed a brand an architect would recognise on a spec sheet and remember in a showroom.

The machined grooves in every panel became the system. The mark is three stacked bars, the type sits on the same rhythm, and each box carries one orange band, the only colour in the identity, so a pallet reads from across a warehouse.
The new packaging shipped with the spring 2026 range. The groove system now runs across spec sheets, the showroom and the website.

/about.title: About, Yassin Farag
/about.description: Yassin Farag is an independent brand and interface designer in Copenhagen.
h2: I design identities, websites and wayfinding for companies whose products are better than their first impression.
p: I grew up in Cairo, studied graphic design there, and spent eight years in studios in Cairo, Amsterdam and Copenhagen before going independent in 2022.
Most of my clients are small teams with one good product and no time to explain it. I work with them directly, usually alone, sometimes with a photographer, developer or copywriter I trust.
Outside client work I collect bus timetables and badly translated signs. That is where most of my opinions about wayfinding come from.

We couldn’t explain our product in a meeting. Yassin made it explain itself on one page. Our sales calls got shorter the week it launched.
He asked better questions about our signage than our architects did. Visitors stopped asking the front desk for directions.
Quiet, fast and stubborn about the right things. The identity he built still holds up three years and two pivots later.
Our app had forty features and no story. He cut the homepage to three sentences and sign-ups doubled in a month.
He works like a good editor. Every decision came with a reason, and every reason held up when the client pushed back.
Three shops, one brand, zero confusion. People find the counter, the menu and the bathroom without asking anyone.
